Even this pipeline, the one that names semantic verification, places manual verification after its automated filters; the review reads this as consistent with the charter's policy that the `@fidelity-auditor`'s back-translation is one more filter feeding the human gate, not the gate itself.

Read together, these abstracts report high automated rates on the authors' chosen benchmarks and budgets, 93.2% at Pass@128 for statement formalization and an Alignment-Selection Score of 99.21%, alongside lower rates on other sets, 22.5% and 66.39%; the review infers that the evidence supports automated drafting at Stage 1 and a reduced manual burden at G-FID (Gao et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2024b).

No abstract reviewed here claims that automation removes the need for a human fidelity check, nor does any test that claim, so keeping G-FID a human gate is the charter's policy, which this evidence neither forces nor contradicts.

Automated statement formalization and alignment evaluation are reported at high rates on the authors' benchmarks and budgets and at lower rates on other sets; they are reported to reduce manual verification, no abstract claims they remove it, and keeping their scores advisory input to G-FID is the charter's policy (Gao et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2024b).
Lean compiler feedback is reported to improve autoformalization accuracy, but no reviewed abstract equates compiling with fidelity (Lu et al. 2024a).

Automated filtering of autoformalized statements is reported by Lean Workbook and FormalMATH, with manual verification after the filters in FormalMATH; the Goedel-Prover abstract describes no filtering (Ying et al. 2024; Lin et al. 2025a; Yu et al. 2025).

The review classifies the Benzmüller line as shallow semantic embedding, a label none of these abstracts uses, with modal operators turned into quantification over possible worlds inside classical higher-order logic; Bentzen instead fixes an explicit object language and proves a completeness theorem about it, the pattern the charter's deep embedding follows.
The review does not infer that automation reported for the higher-order embeddings transfers to a deep embedding in Lean, since none of these abstracts compares the two.

For cross-checking a modal-logic pilot, the evidence offers an S5 completeness proof in Lean 3 and a cube-inclusion verification in Isabelle/HOL; neither is in Lean 4, so each can serve as a reference statement to re-prove rather than a library to import.

Within the inventory, the review distinguishes a semantic embedding in classical higher-order logic, with reported automation, from an explicit object-language formalization with a mechanized completeness proof; the charter's deep embedding follows the second (Benzmüller and Paulson 2013; Bentzen 2021).

Mechanized modal metatheory exists in Lean 3 and Isabelle/HOL, and a Lean 4 logic library exists whose coverage is not established by its retrieved description (Bentzen 2021; Benzmüller, Claus, and Sultana 2015; FormalizedFormalLogic contributors n.d.).

Taken together, the findings support automated checks of meaning, compilation, and search feeding the Lean kernel rather than standing in for it; keeping the human gates alongside those checks is the charter's policy, which these findings neither force nor contradict.
The best-supported implications concern Stages 4 and 5 and the prover-engine registry, where several abstracts describe the mechanism.

Stage 1 evidence is mixed: automated formalization and alignment are reported at high rates on the authors' benchmarks, no retrieved abstract evaluates back-translation as a fidelity check (the Lean Workbook pipeline translates in both directions, but its abstract presents this as data generation and filtering, not as a fidelity test), and the human G-FID gate rests on charter policy rather than on a finding (Gao et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2024b; Ying et al. 2024).
The weakest concern Stage 3 and the handling of TPTP and SMT-LIB results, where the evidence identifies reference works but not their content; the counterexample track has no supporting finding.

Because more than half of the cited works are arXiv preprints and all content evidence is abstract-level, each implication should be re-examined when the Harness Specification cites it, and none validates the harness as a whole.
